deleted.text: Flyway applies the files in sequence order and records each one in the flyway_schema_history table.
All schema changes for a release are collected into one release migration file and applied in the Sunday window, between 02:00 and 04:00 UTC.
The release DBA applies that file by hand with Flyway while the orders application is stopped and a downtime banner is shown to customers.
Application code that depends on the new schema is deployed in the same window, right after the migration succeeds.
Developers add their statements to the release migration file on the release branch, not to a file of their own.
Any statement is allowed, including renames, drops and type changes, because no running code reads the tables while the window is open.
Data backfills go into the same file after the schema statements so that the release DBA can watch them finish.
A statement that is expected to run longer than twenty minutes is flagged in the file header so the window can be planned.
Every change to the release migration file needs approval from one member of the platform data team.
The reviewer checks the SQL for correctness, estimates its running time on a production-sized copy, and adds the estimate to the release checklist.
The release DBA reads the whole file on the Friday before the window and may move statements to the next release if the window would overrun.
On Sunday at 02:00 UTC the release DBA enables the downtime banner and scales the orders application to zero.
The release DBA takes a snapshot of the database.
The release DBA runs Flyway against production and watches its output.
When Flyway reports success, the deploy pipeline releases the new application version.
The release DBA scales the application back up, removes the banner and posts a note in the release channel.
If Flyway stops with an error, the release DBA restores the snapshot taken in step 2 and redeploys the previous application version.
The failed statements are fixed on the release branch and wait for the next Sunday window.
Because the application is offline for the whole procedure, a failure costs only the time of the restore.
Developer
Adds statements to the release migration file and tests them locally
Reviewer
Approves the SQL and estimates its running time
Release DBA
Runs the Sunday window, applies the file and restores on failure
Support lead
Tells customers about the window in advance
On-call engineer
Handles alerts once the application is back up
Every migration runs in the test suite against an empty local database and against a copy of the staging database.
The staging copy is refreshed every Thursday so that the release migration file can be rehearsed on realistic data before the window.
A rehearsal that runs longer than the estimate on the release checklist is reported to the release DBA.
After the window the release DBA compares the row counts of the changed tables with the snapshot and records them on the release checklist.
Query latency dashboards are watched for one hour after the application comes back up.
Any regression is reported in the release channel and handled by the on-call engineer.
Whether the Sunday window should move to Saturday for customers in Asia.
Whether the snapshot can be replaced by point-in-time recovery.

candidates.sentence: The runner learns which migrations have run from the history table, not from comparing the live schema against a model.
We write no down migrations, and every correction ships as a new forward migration.

The deploy pipeline applies pending migrations automatically before it rolls out the new application version, and a contract migration that removes or tightens something ships only once no running version reads the old shape.
Nobody takes the application offline for a schema change, and customers keep placing orders while it is applied.
Migrations are not saved up and applied together at the end of a release, since each one ships with the change that needs it.
An expand migration may add tables, nullable columns, columns with a constant default, indexes, and constraints marked NOT VALID.
Our migrations never build an index in that blocking form and always use the concurrent variant instead.
A rename is carried out as a new column filled by a backfill, rather than as a view that keeps the old name alive.
The old column is dropped by a later contract migration.
On PostgreSQL 11 and later that is not the case, because a constant default is kept in the catalog without touching existing rows.
The reviewer checks that an expand migration is safe for the application version currently in production, and that a contract migration removes only what no deployed version still reads.
There is no Sunday window to book and no release DBA to page before a migration goes out.
The pipeline never rolls out new application code after a migration has failed.
If a migration file has no matching row in the history table while a later file does, Flyway refuses to start and names the missing file.
The test suite also runs the previous application version against the migrated schema to show that an expand migration is safe.
